title: Verifier‑Grounded Generate‑Verify‑Repair for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Paired Mininet Emulation Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents; 400 paired episodes) to evaluate whether a deterministic verifier‑grounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces operationally detectable policy‑violation errors when a hosted LLM produces device configuration sequences from operator intent in a Mininet emulation. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled initial generation per intent reused by both baseline and guarded). Baseline success (no detected policy violation) = 196/200 (98%); guarded success = 200/200 (100%). Paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.02; preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory test). An exploratory paired bootstrap (seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) yields a 95% percentile CI = [0.005, 0.04]. Four verifier‑triggered repairs occurred (total hosted model calls = 204), giving mean extra model calls per intent = 0.02 and mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. All reported numeric values, provider‑call accounting, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are drawn verbatim from the archived execution and analysis bundle. We interpret the preregistered confirmatory result conservatively and discuss construct, internal, and external validity limits and operational implications.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation for network devices promises to reduce repetitive operator labor and speed change delivery, but Large Language Models (LLMs) produce mechanically detectable faults—syntax errors, topology/reachability violations, and ACL/policy mistakes—that can have operational consequences (outages, unintended access) [1], [4]. Closed‑loop generate–verify‑repair (GVR) pipelines pair an LLM generator with a deterministic verifier that checks mechanizable constraints and, when violations occur, requests localized repairs. Prior prototypes across code and domain programs show verifier‑grounded repair can remove many mechanically checkable failures [2], [3], but open questions remain about multi‑vendor generalization, concrete hosted‑LLM cost per avoided violation, and interpretation of paired comparisons when the same initial sample is reused across conditions.

We preregistered study C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 to evaluate a verifier‑grounded GVR pipeline in a controlled Mininet emulation. The experiment exercises three synthetic vendor‑template families and four topology patterns (12 strata), runs a paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one sampled initial generation per intent reused by both baseline and guarded), and audits provider calls and deterministic validator traces. Our primary estimand compares the per‑intent probability of zero operationally detectable violations under guarded (GVR) versus baseline (single‑shot) generation using the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test. Contributions: (i) a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory evaluation at N = 200 across heterogeneous template families, (ii) explicit execution and interpretation under shared_initial_candidate semantics, and (iii) audited provider and repair costing metrics drawn from the execution manifest.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and NetOps‑specific reviews document rapid growth in LLM‑for‑NetOps research while highlighting consistent evaluation gaps: provenance, verifier integration, and limited multi‑vendor emulation evidence [5], [6]. Prototype NetOps experiments and adjacent domain work demonstrate that LLMs can draft device configurations but frequently introduce syntactic, reachability, or policy errors; generate–verify–repair or verifier‑grounded closed loops recur as a practical mitigation pattern in code and domain‑specific program generation [2], [3]. Benchmarks such as NetConfEval illustrate task families for LLM→configuration evaluation but remain task‑limited and often lack provenance‑traced verifier pipelines [4].

The present study is positioned to address the literature gap identified above (limited multi‑vendor, provenance‑traced verifier evaluations) by (a) exercising heterogeneous synthetic vendor templates in an emulator, (b) recording deterministic validator traces that document before/after validation states per episode, and (c) reporting audited provider‑call decomposition so researchers can reconcile cost vs. effect using archived artifacts. We do not claim production readiness, nor do we attribute guarded improvements to prompt engineering because the preregistered design deliberately reused the initial sample across conditions (shared_initial_candidate).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered as C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 prior to any model calls (preregistration SHA‑256 = 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50). The primary confirmatory estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (probability that an intent yields zero operationally detectable violations under guarded minus baseline) tested with the exact McNemar two‑sided test (α = 0.05). Exploratory estimators included a paired bootstrap percentile CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) and descriptive cost metrics (mean extra model calls per intent and mean extra calls per avoided violation).

Sampling, strata, and shared_initial_candidate semantics: N = 200 unique operator intents were deterministically selected and stratified across three vendor‑template families and four topology patterns (12 strata) using the frozen task index profile. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent exactly one initial sampled generation was produced and reused by both baseline and guarded episodes. Under this semantics baseline outcome equals the validator verdict on that shared candidate; guarded outcome equals the final guarded pipeline result after deterministic validation and any permitted repair. The preregistration declared that independent constrained‑prompt arms were not executed; therefore paired differences derive only from deterministic validator/repair actions rather than from independent first‑pass re‑sampling or alternate prompt templates.

Model configuration, temperature notation, and budget: The declared model in archived execution artifacts is gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). The archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; explicit statement: null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Planned budget: planned_episode_count = 400, initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_model_calls = 400.

Deterministic validator and repair policy: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements: (a) syntactic parsing and canonicalization of configuration commands; (b) required‑command sequencing and dependency checks against per‑task workflow policies; (c) reachability/topology verification against the emulated network state; and (d) encoded ACL/policy constraint checks derived from task payloads. The validator emits a binary success = "no detected violations" under the scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation. When violations are detected the guarded pipeline may issue up to one verifier‑triggered repair call: the repair prompt is constructed from the validator's localized diagnostics requesting corrective modifications. Repair calls occur only when the validator reports violations; repair decisions and before/after validator traces are archived per episode.

Scoring, missingness, and statistical plan: Primary analysis used the exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary success indicators (per preregistration). Exclusion rules predeclared that deterministic duplicate prompts or unrecoverable infra failures would be reported and excluded from the primary paired test; ambiguous validator outputs are conservatively treated as violations in the primary analysis. In execution no pairs were excluded and no episodes failed. The preregistered exploratory paired bootstrap (seed = 1729) and descriptive cost accounting were computed and archived. The preregistration also specified a multiplicity plan that treats secondary analyses as exploratory and reports effect sizes with CIs without alpha adjustment.
sections.results:
Execution completeness and raw counts: The run completed per preregistration: planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; complete_pair_count = 200; failed_episode_count = 0. Audited provider accounting (execution manifest) reports hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposed as 200 shared_initial_generation events and 4 repair calls; cache_hit_count = 0.

Paired outcomes and contingency: The analysis paired contingency table (archived analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 196 (both succeed), n10 = 4 (guarded succeed, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline succeed), n00 = 0 (both fail). Baseline success rate = 196/200 = 0.98; guarded success rate = 200/200 = 1.0; paired point estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.02.

Confirmatory test and exploratory interval: The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory result; do not reject at α = 0.05). The archived exploratory paired bootstrap (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) produced a 95% percentile CI for the paired risk difference = [0.005, 0.04] (bootstrap artifacts archived). We caution that when discordant pair counts (n10 + n01) are small, resampling intervals can be unstable; the preregistered McNemar exact test is the formal confirmatory inference.

Repair and cost accounting: Four verifier‑triggered repairs were invoked across the 200 intents (repair_calls = 4). Total hosted model calls = 204 (200 shared initial + 4 repairs), yielding mean hosted model calls per intent = 1.02 and mean extra calls per intent due to repairs = 0.02. In the archived contingency each repair corrected one baseline failure in the recorded discordant pairs; arithmetic implies mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. These provider counts and stage breakdowns are the audited values from the execution manifest and deterministic reconciliation artifacts.

Representative example episodes: Representative scoring artifacts show the shared initial candidate reused by both conditions. For example, a representative task's shared initial configuration (representative task entry) is the sequence: "interface edge2 admin down\ninterface edge2 vlan 40\ninterface edge2 admin up\ninterface edge1 admin down". For discordant episodes the validator_trace.validation_before recorded a detected violation and validator_trace.validation_after recorded that a repair was applied and the final configuration passed full_intent_constraint_validation. These per‑episode traces and normalized configurations substantiate the contingency counts and repair accounting reported above.

Statistical diagnostics and power context: The preregistered power plan targeted detecting a 10 percentage point absolute reduction with N ≈ 157 (McNemar approximation); N = 200 provided margin for stratified descriptions. The observed baseline failure prevalence (2%) is lower than some planning scenarios, reducing power to detect small absolute improvements; this explains the non‑significant McNemar result despite a positive point estimate and small discordant count (4). We therefore present the p‑value as the formal hypothesis test result and treat the bootstrap CI as supplemental magnitude context.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation under shared_initial_candidate semantics: Because execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled initial generation per intent shared across baseline and guarded), any paired improvement derives only from deterministic validator/repair actions and not from differences in the initial sampled candidate or prompt templates. The preregistration explicitly declared that independent constrained‑prompt arms were not executed; therefore readers should not attribute guarded improvements to prompt engineering or distinct first‑pass sampling.

Construct validity limits: The deterministic validator expresses syntactic, reachability/topology, and encoded ACL/policy checks but cannot detect higher‑order semantic misinterpretations that are not formalized in its rule set. Remaining undetected semantic errors are a residual uncertainty: the validator's false‑negative risk for non‑mechanizable specification misinterpretations remains unquantified. Expanding the verifier ontology is a necessary direction to reduce this residual.

Internal and conclusion validity: The preregistered missingness and exclusion rules were followed; no episodes were excluded and all deterministic consistency checks passed in reconciliation artifacts. Small discordant counts limit statistical precision and make resampling intervals less stable; the exact McNemar test is therefore the appropriate confirmatory procedure under our paired design. The observed effect (2 percentage points) corrected all recorded baseline violations in this workload but did not reach the preregistered α threshold for significance.

Operational implications and bounded claims: Within the constrained Mininet emulation, synthetic vendor templates, and the validator's encoded rules, a small repair budget (four repairs) eliminated the mechanically detectable baseline violations at low model‑call overhead. This artifact‑grounded outcome suggests that when a suitable deterministic verifier provides localized actionable diagnostics, bounded repair budgets can remove many mechanically checkable faults in template‑driven emulated settings. We do not claim generalization to production hardware, alternative prompt families, other LLMs, or coverage of semantic errors outside the verifier's rule set.

Recommendations grounded in archived evidence: (1) broaden deterministic verifier coverage to encode additional semantic/policy ontologies and measure residual false negatives; (2) run paired designs that allow independent multi‑sample initial generations to isolate prompt or sampling effects (not executed here); (3) replicate across multiple hosted models and versions to assess robustness to provider nondeterminism; and (4) preserve provenance tracing for provider calls and validator traces to enable external audit. Each recommendation follows directly from execution artifacts and manifested limitations.
sections.conclusion:
We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents; shared_initial_candidate semantics) to measure whether a deterministic verifier plus bounded repair reduces mechanically detectable policy violations for intent→configuration tasks in a Mininet emulation. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test did not reject at α = 0.05 (p = 0.125). Guarded GVR invoked four repairs and corrected the four observed baseline violations at low model‑call overhead (mean extra calls per intent = 0.02), yielding a paired risk difference estimate of 0.02 and an exploratory paired bootstrap CI = [0.005, 0.04] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). These artifact‑grounded results indicate that when a deterministic verifier can express and check relevant constraints and provide localized feedback, a small repair budget can eliminate mechanically detectable policy violations in similar template‑based emulated settings. The results do not establish production readiness, multi‑model generality, or coverage for semantic errors outside the validator. Future preregistered, provenance‑traced evaluations should expand verifier coverage, evaluate multiple hosted models, and compare independent multi‑sample baselines.

References
[1] R. Mondal, A. Tang, R. Beckett, T. Millstein, and G. Varghese, "What do LLMs need to Synthesize Correct Router Configurations?", in Proc. ACM, 2023, doi: 10.1145/3626111.3628194.
[2] R. Cadenas, "Convergent Correctness in Stochastic Code Generation: A Generate‑Verify‑Repair Architecture for Deterministic Validation of Autonomous AI Coding Agents in Regulated Environments", SSRN, 2026, doi: 10.2139/ssrn.6754899.
[3] Z. Ding, "Executable but Wrong: Verifier‑Grounded Contracts and Counterexamples for LLM‑Generated Music Programs", 2026, doi: 10.31224/7995.
[4] C. Wang, M. Scazzariello, A. Farshin, S. Ferlin, D. Kostić, and M. Chiesa, "NetConfEval: Can LLMs Facilitate Network Configuration?", Proc. ACM, 2024, doi: 10.1145/3656296.
[5] S. Y. Long et al., "A Survey on Intelligent Network Operations and Performance Optimization Based on Large Language Models", IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials, 2025, doi: 10.1109/comst.2025.3526606.
[6] L. Zhang et al., "A Survey of AIOps in the Era of Large Language Models", Proc. ACM, 2025, doi: 10.1145/3746635.

Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Preregistration: C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 (SHA‑256 = 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50) was recorded before any model calls. Human role: a human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; after the lock the AI autonomously performed literature verification, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, peer review, revision, and manuscript drafting; no human manually edited technical manuscript content after the autonomy lock. Sampling semantics: execution used shared_initial_candidate (one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and reused by both baseline and guarded); archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset (null/unset is not evidence of deterministic provider sampling and does not imply temperature = 0). Provider accounting (audited): hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposed as 200 shared initial generations + 4 repair calls. Reported numbers and analysis artifacts are drawn from the archived execution and analysis bundles.
limitations: Scope limited to Mininet‑style emulation with synthetic, provenance‑traced intent→configuration tasks; results do not generalize directly to production hardware or live operations.
Single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) evaluated; multi‑model generality is not established.

Deterministic validator coverage limited to mechanically checkable errors (syntax, reachability, ACL/policy encodings); higher‑level semantic or specification misinterpretations outside the validator may remain undetected.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics imply observed paired differences derive only from verifier‑triggered repair; this design does not measure effects of alternative prompting strategies or independent multi‑sample candidate selection.

Observed confirmatory effect (2 percentage points) did not reach statistical significance at α = 0.05 for N = 200 (exact McNemar p = 0.125); low baseline failure prevalence (2%) reduced power to detect small absolute improvements under some preregistered scenarios.
